items.name: Bhojpuri / Awadhi flavour for Bihar and UP audiences
items.one_line: Sprinkle Bhojpuri or Awadhi words, idioms and rhythm into Hindi copy for eastern UP, Bihar and Jharkhand audiences, written in Devanagari.

sources.title: Bhojpuri language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: spoken in eastern UP, western Bihar, northwestern Jharkhand and diaspora; about 50.5 million speakers in Census 2011 with more counted under Hindi; Devanagari is the main script (historically Kaithi); large cinema and music industry

sources.title: Awadhi language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: spoken in the Awadh region of UP; grouped under Hindi by the government; Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi

items.note: Flavour, not full dialect, unless the writer is a native speaker: a full Bhojpuri script written by a non-speaker reads as mockery. Satire using a dialect to mock its speakers is a risk.

items.name: Simplified English for subtitles and captions
items.one_line: Condense spoken English to a readable line: short lines, clean line breaks, numbers rule, reading-speed limit.

sources.title: Netflix English (USA) Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: 42 characters per line, max two lines; up to 20 characters per second for adults, 17 for children; numbers 0-10 written out, above 10 as digits; break after punctuation and before conjunctions/prepositions; favour reduction and condensing for reading speed

items.note: These are Netflix's numbers; social-platform caption limits are the platform worker's kind.

items.name: Global / plain English for non-native readers
items.one_line: Short, literal, idiom-free English that survives machine translation and second-language reading.

sources.title: Microsoft Style Guide: Global communications
sources.supports: assume readers whose first language is not English and content that will be machine-translated; defines translation vs localization; points to plainlanguage.gov and the Global English Style Guide (Kohl, 2008)

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: voice and tone
sources.supports: global audience: simple consistent language, minimal culture-specific references, no figurative language

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7
sources.supports: avoid slang, colloquialisms and obscure phrasing in source text: hard to translate, can offend

items.note: The right base text when the same script will be translated into Hindi or regional languages.

items.name: English for Gulf NRI audiences
items.one_line: Indian-English copy aimed at the large Indian workforce in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain.

sources.title: Ministry of External Affairs (India): Population of Overseas Indians (table, undated in the text layer)
sources.supports: NRIs: UAE 3,419,875; Saudi Arabia 2,592,166; Kuwait 1,028,274; Oman 779,351; Qatar 745,775; Bahrain 323,292

items.note: Audience size is sourced; no style guide for this variety was found, so writing rules here are unsourced. A search summary gave different country figures from the MEA table; use the MEA table.

items.name: Hindi in Devanagari (standard)
items.one_line: Standard written Hindi: aap-form politeness, purna viram (।) not a dot or pipe, Latin digits by default, day-month-year dates, brand names kept as-is.

sources.title: Mozilla style guide: Hindi (hi-IN)
sources.supports: use आप/यह/वह not तुम/ये/वे; avoid curt imperatives (ढूँढें not ढूँढो); purna viram (।) not '.' or '|'; Latin digits 0-9 not ०-९; brand names neither translated nor transliterated; dates like 25 सितम्बर 2016

sources.title: Danda (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: danda U+0964 and double danda U+0965; Hindi uses them together with Western punctuation

sources.title: Hindustani language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: standard Hindi is the Sanskritised register of Hindustani; grammar and core vocabulary are shared with Urdu

items.note: Mozilla's 'aap' rule is for UI/formal copy; reels and Hinglish creator copy often use 'tum'/'tu' by design (that is a tone choice). Type the danda as U+0964, never a pipe or the letter l.

items.name: Romanising Hindi: Hunterian, IAST/ISO 15919 and informal Hinglish spelling
items.one_line: Pick the romanisation for the job: Hunterian for names and places, IAST/ISO 15919 when it must be reversible, informal Hinglish spelling for social copy.

sources.title: Devanagari transliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Hunterian is India's national romanisation for geographic names but does not mark retroflex vs dental; IAST is losslessly reversible; ITRANS and Harvard-Kyoto are ASCII schemes; informal romanised Hindi dominates online

sources.title: International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: IAST diacritics and its relation to ISO 15919

items.note: Social copy never uses diacritics; keep one informal spelling per word across a series (a house spelling list).

items.name: Hindi and Hinglish SEO
items.one_line: Write Hindi pages for how Indians actually search: Devanagari pages ranked on visible text, Roman-script Hinglish queries, one language per page.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites
sources.supports: Google determines page language from visible content, not the lang attribute or URL; separate URLs per language; avoid side-by-side translations

sources.title: IAMAI and Kantar, Internet in India 2024
sources.supports: 870 million users (98% of internet users) accessed the internet in Indic languages in 2024; 57% of urban users prefer Indic-language content; online search is among the activities done in Indic languages (chart)

sources.title: Search Engine Journal: Google Updates Indian Searches With Translated Results (2021)
sources.supports: Google translates English result titles and snippets into Hindi and other Indian languages because local-language content is scarce

sources.title: Hinglish (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: a cited YouTube-comment study found Romanised Hindi far more common than Devanagari; Google supports Hinglish in Gboard and Search

items.note: Research both scripts for each keyword (e.g. 'sarkari yojana' and 'सरकारी योजना'). Exact Indic search-share numbers by script were not found in a primary source.

items.name: Hindi subtitles and on-screen text
items.one_line: Hindi timed text: short lines, reading-speed limit, small numbers written out, English words transliterated into Devanagari.

sources.title: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: 42 characters per line; up to 22 characters per second for adults, 18 for children; numbers 1-10 written out, above 10 as digits; English words in a Hindi line transliterated; on-screen text only when plot-pertinent

items.note: For reel burn-in captions use the same reading-speed logic; keep Devanagari conjuncts on one line (do not break inside a word).

items.name: Hindi for voice-over and TTS
items.one_line: Write Hindi scripts so a TTS engine says them right: numbers, dates, symbols and abbreviations spelled out as words, English terms in Devanagari, punctuation for pauses.

sources.title: Raj, Sarkar, Pammi, Yuvaraj, Bansal, Prahallad, Black: Text Processing for Text-to-Speech Systems in Indian Languages (SSW6, 2007)
sources.supports: covers font-to-akshara mapping, pronunciation rules for aksharas, and normalising non-standard words (numbers, abbreviations, dates, currency, addresses) into standard words before synthesis

sources.title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech: SSML
sources.supports: say-as (cardinal, ordinal, characters, date, currency, telephone), sub alias and break let a script force how a token is read and where pauses fall

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024
sources.supports: has a chapter on uniform spelling of Hindi number words (संख्यावाचक शब्दों की एकरूपता), the reference for writing numbers out

items.note: Write 2,500 as ढाई हज़ार, ₹ as रुपये, % as प्रतिशत, PM as पीएम or प्रधानमंत्री. Local pipeline observation (unsourced, from this machine's F5 bake-off notes): F5 tends to drop a line's first word, so a sacrificial lead word and a per-word ASR read-back are used; treat that as engine-specific.

items.name: Everyday Hindustani register (bolchaal Hindi)
items.one_line: The spoken middle register shared by Hindi and Urdu speakers: common words, no heavy Sanskrit or Persian, the language of Bollywood dialogue.

sources.title: Hindustani language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: colloquial Hindustani avoids high-register Sanskrit- or Perso-Arabic-derived words; Bollywood films use this neutral vernacular

items.note: Default register for Hindi reels and VO. Swap tatsam words (e.g. formal Sanskrit terms) for the everyday word unless the piece is devotional or official.

items.name: Hinglish in Devanagari (English words in Hindi script)
items.one_line: Hindi sentences that keep everyday English words but write them in Devanagari (मोबाइल, डॉक्टर, ऑफ़र).

sources.title: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: English words used in a mostly Hindi line of dialogue need no identifiers but should be transliterated (into Devanagari)

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024 edition
sources.supports: standard Devanagari includes the ardhachandra sign ऑ for English sounds, with डॉक्टर as the example (text layer of the PDF is partly garbled; read from the alphabet section)

sources.title: Bali et al. 2014, 'I am borrowing ya mixing?' (ACL CodeSwitch workshop)
sources.supports: the common pattern is a Hindi grammatical frame with English words inserted (23.7% of Hindi matrices vs 7.2% the other way); borrowing vs mixing is a continuum

items.note: Use ऑ for the English 'o' in doctor/office/coffee. Keep brand names in Latin script (Mozilla hi-IN rule). This is the script TTS engines read best for Hindi VO; Roman Hinglish confuses Hindi voices.

items.name: Hinglish in Roman script
items.one_line: Hindi-English code-mixing typed in Latin letters, the dominant script for Hindi speakers online.

sources.title: Hinglish (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Hinglish = code-switching between colloquial Hindi and English, in writing usually Romanised; a cited YouTube-comment study found Romanised Hindi far ahead of Devanagari; Google added Hinglish support to Gboard and Search

items.note: No standard spelling exists, so pick one spelling per word and keep it (hai/hain, nahi/nahin, kya). Spell for how the audience types, not scholarly transliteration.

items.name: Indian number, currency and date formats
items.one_line: Lakh/crore and 2-digit grouping (12,34,56,789), the rupee sign U+20B9, and day-month-year dates for Indian readers.

sources.title: Indian numbering system (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: lakh = 100,000, crore = 10 million; digits grouped in pairs after the first three; Indian publications use lakh/crore for rupee amounts, international units for foreign currency

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7 (Govt of India, L10N-eGov, Jan 2014)
sources.supports: rupee sign must be stored as U+20B9; India date shown as DD-MM-YY; English (Latin) digits recommended where numbers are computed

sources.title: Mozilla style guide: Hindi (hi-IN)
sources.supports: Hindi dates written day-month-year with the month in Devanagari; times with colon

items.note: Never write 'Rs 10 lakhs crore'-style hybrids; choose lakh/crore (Indian readers) or million/billion (global) per piece. Applies to English, Hindi and Hinglish copy.

items.name: Indian English
items.one_line: British-based spelling with -ise, lakh/crore for Indian money, and India-specific vocabulary that global readers may not know.

sources.title: Indian English (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: follows British spelling; lakh/crore in formal publications; Indianisms such as prepone, do the needful, pass out (graduate), emphatic 'only'

sources.title: American and British English spelling differences (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: India strongly prefers -ise over -ize

items.note: Indianisms are fine for Indian audiences but flag them (prepone, do the needful, 'multiple equipments') when the reader is global; that is a mistake list for the card.

items.name: Localisation QA
items.one_line: Check translated or transcreated copy against an error typology before it ships: terminology, accuracy, conventions, style, locale, audience fit, layout.

sources.title: MQM (Multidimensional Quality Metrics) error typology
sources.supports: seven top-level dimensions: terminology, accuracy, linguistic conventions, style, locale conventions, audience appropriateness, design and markup; MQM Core vs Full

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7 (Govt of India, Jan 2014)
sources.supports: Unicode storage, rupee sign U+20B9, locale date format, Latin digits for computed numbers, avoid slang and disputed maps in source content

items.note: For Indic text add script checks: danda typed correctly, matras and conjuncts render in the target font, nuqta consistent, no Latin lookalike characters.

items.name: Regional Indian languages (overview)
items.one_line: India's next-largest languages after Hindi, each with its own script; content for them is transcreated by a native writer, not run through Hindi.

sources.title: Languages of India (Wikipedia, Census 2011 table)
sources.supports: first-language speakers 2011: Bengali 97.2M (Bengali script), Marathi 83.0M (Devanagari), Telugu 81.1M, Tamil 69.0M, Gujarati 55.5M, Urdu 50.8M (Perso-Arabic), Kannada 43.7M, Odia 37.5M, Malayalam 34.8M, Punjabi 33.1M (Gurmukhi); 22 Eighth Schedule languages

sources.title: IAMAI and Kantar, Internet in India 2024
sources.supports: 98% of internet users accessed Indic-language content in 2024; urban preference split by language is charted

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7
sources.supports: 22 official languages and 12 scripts; Unicode and CLDR locale data per language

items.note: Marathi shares Devanagari with Hindi but not its spelling or vocabulary; never pass Hindi off as Marathi. Sources found support script and speaker counts only, so writing rules per language are left to native reviewers (one combined item for that reason).

items.name: Sanskrit shlokas in devotional content (Devanagari + IAST)
items.one_line: Quote shlokas in Devanagari with danda/double-danda verse marks and, when romanised, use lossless IAST diacritics.

sources.title: International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: IAST is a lossless romanisation: macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, ś ṣ ṃ ḥ; ISO 15919 follows it closely; standard in scholarly publishing

sources.title: Danda (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: in Sanskrit, danda and double danda are the only punctuation: double danda closes a verse, single danda a half-verse

items.note: Copy the shloka from a reliable edition and cite chapter/verse; a single wrong matra changes meaning. For reels, show Devanagari plus a plain Hindi/English meaning rather than IAST.

items.name: Transcreation (vs translation)
items.one_line: Recreate the message for a new language and culture so it lands with the same intent, tone and emotion, changing words, references and imagery as needed.

sources.title: Transcreation (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: keeps intent, style, tone and context; adapts imagery and culture; used in marketing, ads, games; Spider-Man: India as an example

sources.title: Microsoft Style Guide: Global communications
sources.supports: translation changes the language; localization adapts content to a locale's language, cultural and political expectations and is done by people who know that culture

sources.title: KPMG and Google, Indian Languages: Defining India's Internet (April 2017)
sources.supports: Indian-language users show higher propensity to respond to digital ads in their own language and see local-language content as more reliable

items.note: Hooks, puns, rhymes and CTAs need transcreation; legal text, specs and prices need literal translation plus review.

items.name: UK English
items.one_line: British spelling: -our, -ise (or Oxford -ize), -re, doubled l (travelled), licence/practice as nouns vs license/practise as verbs.

sources.title: American and British English spelling differences (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: British patterns; Oxford spelling keeps -ize; Commonwealth countries normally follow British usage

items.note: Oxford spelling (-ize with other British forms) is a legitimate house style; pick one and apply it throughout.

items.name: Urdu-influenced Hindi (shayari register, nuqta)
items.one_line: Hindi coloured with Perso-Arabic vocabulary for shayari, romance and poetic captions; nuqta letters (क़ ख़ ग़ ज़ फ़) mark the borrowed sounds.

sources.title: Nuqta (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: nuqta (U+093C) marks Perso-Arabic sounds in Devanagari; its use in Hindi is optional and inconsistent; precomposed nuqta letters also exist

sources.title: Hindustani language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Urdu register draws on Persian and Arabic vocabulary; grammar is shared with Hindi

items.note: Nuqta changes meaning in a few pairs and matters for TTS pronunciation; be consistent within one piece and prefer the combining U+093C sequence or precomposed letters consistently, not a mix.

items.name: US English
items.one_line: American spelling and conventions: -or, -ize, -er, single l (traveled), license for noun and verb, month-day-year dates.

sources.title: American and British English spelling differences (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: American patterns: color, organize, center, traveled, license (noun and verb), anemia

items.note: Use for US-market clients, SaaS docs written to a US style guide, and Google Ads aimed at the US. Do not mix with UK/Indian spellings inside one piece.
